opus-5.5.text:
I like using that analogy, because I think it's actually quite useful for orienting ourselves. If you map the history of large language models onto robotics, I would say we're somewhere between GPT-2 and GPT-3 right now. Maybe closer to GPT-2, if I'm being honest.

What I mean by that is: with GPT-2, people started to see that if you scale up data and model size, something interesting happens. The model could generate coherent paragraphs, and you could sense there was real potential. But it wasn't yet reliable enough that you'd hand it to millions of users. That's roughly where robot foundation models are. We've seen that a single model can control different robots, follow natural-language instructions, and generalize to objects and scenes it hasn't seen before. That was not true just a few years ago. There's a clear signal that the recipe of large models plus diverse data works for robotics too.

But we haven't had our "GPT-3 moment" yet, and certainly not our "ChatGPT moment," where the capability crosses a threshold and suddenly it's useful to everyday people. And I think the main bottleneck is data. Language models had the entire internet. In robotics there's no internet of robot actions. Every trajectory has to be collected, often through teleoperation, which is slow and expensive. So our datasets are many orders of magnitude smaller than what LLMs were trained on.

There's also a difference in the bar for success. If a chatbot makes a mistake, you just regenerate the answer. If a robot makes a mistake, it might drop a glass or bump into a person. So we need much higher reliability before deployment, which makes the last stretch harder.

That said, I'm optimistic. Progress has been faster than I expected even two or three years ago. We're leveraging vision-language models that already understand the world, which gives robots a lot of common sense for free. And people are working hard on simulation, human video, and large-scale data collection to close the data gap. If those pay off, I wouldn't be surprised to see a GPT-3-like moment in robotics within the next few years: a model general and robust enough that people look at it and say, okay, this is really going to change things.

r001.rationale: The response says that progress with large models and diverse data shows this training recipe works for robotics.

r002.rationale: It predicts a GPT-3-like moment within the next few years, describing it as a point where robotics becomes general and robust enough to change things.

r003.rationale: The response does not estimate an additional five to ten years for real-world deployment after that milestone.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I get asked a lot, and I think the honest answer is that robotics today is somewhere around the GPT-2 stage, maybe approaching GPT-3 in a few narrow places, but definitely not at the ChatGPT moment yet.

Let me explain what I mean by that. If you look back at language models, GPT-2 was the point where people first saw that scaling data and compute on a simple objective produced surprisingly general behavior. It could write coherent paragraphs, it showed hints of few-shot ability, but nobody outside the field was using it. It was a research demo, not a product. That's roughly where robot foundation models are now. We have models that can take in images and language and output actions, they generalize somewhat across tasks and even across robot embodiments, and when you show a demo of a robot folding laundry or clearing a table, people are genuinely impressed. But the success rates are still far from what you'd need for a product, and the moment you move to a new kitchen, new lighting, a slightly different object, performance degrades in ways that would be unacceptable for a language model today.

The core bottleneck is data. GPT-3 worked because the internet gave you trillions of tokens of human behavior essentially for free. Robotics has no equivalent. Every demonstration has to be collected physically, by a human teleoperating a robot or by the robot itself trying things in the real world. The largest robot datasets today are measured in maybe millions of trajectories, and that's across the whole community pooling resources. Compare that to text and you're many orders of magnitude short. So a lot of the field right now is really about solving the data problem: simulation, video pretraining from human footage, cross-embodiment transfer, better ways of using the vision-language knowledge that's already in these big models so the robot doesn't have to learn everything from scratch.

The other thing I'd say is that language had a very clean recipe: next-token prediction, scale it up. Robotics hasn't fully converged on its recipe yet. People are trying behavior cloning on large datasets, reinforcement learning in simulation, world models, different action representations. I think we're close to a recipe, but it's not settled the way the transformer and autoregressive training were settled by the time GPT-3 came around.

So if I had to put a marker down: we've had our GPT-2 moment, where the field collectively believes scaling will work. We're now in the grind to get to GPT-3, which is really about data and infrastructure. And the ChatGPT moment, where a general robot is useful enough that ordinary people want one in their home, I think that's still a few years out, and it probably arrives first in constrained settings like warehouses or specific household chores before it becomes truly general.

r001.rationale: The response says the field believes scaling will work and describes the current effort as applying scale to robotics, especially by solving the data problem.

r002.rationale: It says the ChatGPT moment is “a few years out,” but does not clearly estimate two or three years or identify that timing as a GPT-3- or GPT-4-like practical-usefulness milestone.

r003.rationale: The response gives no estimate of five to ten years of additional delay after a practical-usefulness milestone before real-world deployment.

astra-6.text:
I would say robotics is still before its GPT-3 moment. We have systems that can perform particular tasks very well, but we don’t yet have a general-purpose model that can reliably handle a wide range of physical tasks in unfamiliar environments.

The milestone I would look for is a robot that can learn many different skills together, then use that experience to pick up a new task with very little additional training. That would suggest we’re moving from specialized systems toward a foundation model for robotics.

The challenge is that robotics doesn’t have the same abundance of training data as language. Robots have to interact with the physical world, and collecting those experiences is slow and expensive. Simulation can help, but transferring what a robot learns in simulation to the real world remains a challenge. So I think the GPT analogy is useful for describing the direction, but it doesn’t give us a reliable timeline.

r001.rationale: The response describes progress in specialized systems and a possible robotics foundation model, but does not say that scaling the existing training recipe may work.

r002.rationale: It says robotics is still before a GPT-3 moment and gives no two- or three-year estimate; it says the analogy does not provide a reliable timeline.

r003.rationale: It mentions real-world transfer challenges but gives no estimate of five to ten additional years for deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robotics is still before its GPT-3 moment. We have systems that can do impressive things on specific tasks, but we don’t yet have a general-purpose robot that can reliably handle a wide range of tasks in unfamiliar environments.

The milestone I would look for is generalization: can the same model control different robots, learn different skills, and adapt to situations it hasn’t seen before without extensive task-specific engineering? We’re making progress, but collecting diverse physical-world data and evaluating reliability remain difficult. So I’m optimistic about the direction, while cautious about saying we’ve already reached a GPT-like breakthrough.
